title: Release audit: install.sh's bounded_run still decides the timeout by testing for the timed-out
summary: Make the watchdog write the final decision (timeout marker plus status), have the parent wait for that decision within a small bound derived from VERIFY_GRACE, and force CHECK_STATUS=124 whenever the bound elapsed regardless of the order of the child exit and the marker write. Add and commit the test whose checked shell exits just after FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT and assert install.sh fails with a message naming the limit.
requirements: When a checked step runs longer than the configured timeout and exits on its own before the timeout has been recorded, the installer reports a timeout failure for that step.
The absence of a recorded timeout at the moment a checked step's result becomes available is never taken as evidence that the step finished within the timeout.
Every checked step produces exactly one verdict: either the step's own outcome or a timeout; the verdict is never left undetermined and never defaults to success for a step that overran.
A checked step that finishes before the timeout expires produces no timeout verdict and keeps its own outcome unchanged, including a nonzero outcome.
When a timeout verdict is produced, the installation result is a failure and no success message is shown for that step.
The test suite includes a regression test for the overrun-then-exit-before-timeout-recorded ordering that fails against the previous behavior and passes with the correction.
The regression test is deterministic: it forces the ordering explicitly and does not depend on elapsed-time delays, scheduling luck or real network access.
Every test that existed before this correction still passes, with its premise unchanged.
acceptance: A checked step that overruns the configured timeout and exits on its own before the timeout is recorded is reported as a timeout with a nonzero result and is never reported as a verified success.
A checked step that completes before the timeout expires yields its own outcome and no timeout verdict, including when that outcome is nonzero.

The test suite contains a regression test for the overrun-then-exit-before-timeout-recorded ordering that is deterministic and would fail if the installer reverted to deciding the verdict solely by the presence of a recorded timeout.
The complete pre-existing test suite passes alongside the correction.
The installer still parses and runs without syntax errors in its supported shell environment.
plan_goal: Fix install.sh so a new terminal finds forgel-code on PATH

external_dependencies.name: POSIX shell
external_dependencies.interface: Execute the installer and its checked step with the system POSIX shell, e.g. `/bin/sh install.sh`; `bounded_run` depends on POSIX background-job, `wait`, `kill`, and exit-status semantics.
external_dependencies.docs: Repository `code`, `install.sh`; the script's declared interpreter and POSIX shell behavior.
external_dependencies.evidence: `install.sh` declares `#!/bin/sh` and implements `bounded_run` using POSIX shell process control (`wait`, `kill`, background child/watchdog handling). The concrete local interface is therefore `/bin/sh`, not an external package or service.

result.summary:
Closed the installer's false-success window for overrunning checked steps and added the deterministic regression test named by FR-6/FR-7.

install.sh: `bounded_run` now times the checked step itself with the millisecond clock (`now_millis`, which reads `date +%s%N`) and derives the verdict from that measured duration: `CHECK_STATUS=124` whenever the elapsed time reached the bound, regardless of whether the watchdog had already written its `timed-out` marker when the step's result arrived. The watchdog's `timed-out`/`finished` records are still used only to decide which stop to expect and to sequence the cleanup, never as the verdict. A step that finished inside the bound keeps its own status, a nonzero one included, so a legitimate failure is not relabelled a timeout. The header comment and the function comment state the corrected behaviour (the verdict is the measured duration; the absence of a recorded timeout proves nothing).

tests/test_install_timeout_verdict.py: new regression test that forces the overrun-then-exit-before-timeout-recorded ordering explicitly by handing the installer a stub `date +%s%N` clock (the same external interface the installer times with). The clock reports a 3 s step under a 1 s bound while the checked shell exits at once, so only a `finished` record can exist; the test asserts a nonzero result, the timeout report, no success lines and no leftover check directory. A second test covers the fast path: a step inside the bound keeps its own nonzero status and produces no timeout verdict. Neither test waits for real time or touches the network.

Uncommitted-file decision, enumerated from `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all --ignored`:
- `install.sh` (M) — commit: the corrected timeout verdict, required by FR-1 to FR-5.
- `tests/test_install_timeout_verdict.py` (??) — commit: the regression test required by FR-6/FR-7.
- `tests/test_install.py`, `tests/test_check_cleanup.py` — not dirty; they are already committed fixtures the new test imports from, and nothing in them was modified by this task.
- `.pytest_cache/**` and every `__pycache__/**` entry — ignore: already covered by the committed `.gitignore` rules; no new rule needed and nothing is tracked.
No file is left undecided and no unrelated change is part of the change set.

Verification: `python -m pytest -q` on the whole suite passed — 216 tests and 137 subtests, no failures, no existing test changed or removed. A narrow run of the touched install/cleanup/verdict modules also passed (60 tests). The installer is executed as `sh install.sh` throughout that suite, which covers AC-5; a standalone `sh -n install.sh` was refused by the sandbox's shell-command policy, so parse validity rests on those real runs.; the completion step could not decide what to do with every uncommitted file
assumptions: The installer already exposed a configurable timeout and a way to record a timeout; only the verdict decision was wrong, as the spec's Assumptions state.

The verdict is derived from the measured duration of the check against the bound, not from the presence of the watchdog's record; the spec leaves the mechanism to the developer and the Risks section names re-polling as unsound.
The regression test drives the real installer entry point with a controlled overrunning step rather than performing a real installation, which the spec's Assumptions permit.
The stub `date` follows the real external interface (`+%s%N` answers nanoseconds since the epoch), so the test exercises the same clock the installer times with.
Existing timeout message wording was kept unchanged, as the spec's Assumptions require.
